body: Are you sure you can guarantee *all* these places will be safe? That `get_viewport` will *never* return `nullptr` here? Also the reasoning behind it here is that it will fail silently when called in the wrong place, but now it will *crash* when called in the wrong place instead, which is worse IMO

Your commit seems not to be linked to your GitHub account. See: [Why are my commits linked to the wrong user?](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/committing-changes-to-your-project/troubleshooting-commits/why-are-my-commits-linked-to-the-wrong-user) for more info.

I do not guarantee, but I do trust the programmers using `accept_event` to be not using it for no reason (i.e. without an event given by viewport in the tree), and that they wouldn't manually call an input method on a control that could be outside of a tree without checking. I think it's a pretty reasonable expectation the viewport exists in all the places I changed, and if it doesn't, then I consider it already a problem which can be trivial to solve going forward, unlike with `accept_event`. If for some reason the developers can't be trusted, I can re-add the calls to `accept_event`, but I still believe it should not be used in future code, hence the deprecation.

I really cannot fathom why code containing `accept_event()` or `get_viewport()->set_input_as_handled()` would ever be reached in the first place if the control is not inside the tree and with a viewport, because that would mean they're calling calling it without having an event, which makes no sense to do.

Just as you would not use `draw_*` outside of the draw event, you would not use `accept_event` or `set_input_as_handled` outside of the input propagation event, which _guarantees_ a tree and a viewport. It is no different. I don't see why controls should be specially exempt from requiring logic and reason to handle an input, when other non-control nodes are fine with using `get_viewport()->set_input_as_handled()` where it makes sense to do so.

The difference is that it won't crash if you do those things, the difference here is that `get_viewport()->set_input_as_handled()` is not a drop-in replacement, and for inexperienced users (especially as we add functionality to warn users in the editor if they use deprecated methods, a PR that is likely to get merged soon) we'll have users switching without necessarily knowing to make sure the code won't crash, `accept_event()` is a useful shorthand that *also* guarantees safety and won't break things if used "incorrectly"

This would also be very disruptive, forcing a *lot* of documentation and tutorials to be updated, and creating confusion for people migrating from previous versions, for no real strong reason IMO, there's nothing wrong with the current method, so removing it feels very disruptive to me, and I think we should improve the method if there's something wrong with it

I can understand a novice accidentally using a draw method outside of the draw event, just looking at the documentation on the draw functions isn't enough to deduce you couldn't use it inside of _ready for instance. But one does not "accidentally" handle an input event, outside of the tree no less, without seriously going out of ones way and ignoring all documentation on the matter. There can be no honest mistake about it. It is completely illogical.
And if they see an error that `get_viewport()` is null, it is pretty obvious where to start looking for what they did wrong. Whereas `accept_input()` will just leave them confused as to why the inputevent is still propagating. But neither are ever likely to occur without serious mental gymnastics.

That just means we should make a clearer error IMO, also they won't get an error if it's somehow uncaught in release, the game will just crash, if the specific case isn't caught in testing

I agree that it won't occur without exceptional cases, which is just another argument for not removing a hugely useful method, especially since this is will cause a (though arguably minor) reduction in performance, especially if used a lot

```gdscript
if is_inside_tree():
    get_viewport().set_input_as_handled()
# better yet:
if get_viewport():
    get_viewport().set_input_as_handled()
```
Does not seem like a hugely useful method. Especially considering everything about input events depends on there being a viewport and the node being in the tree already. The odds of the user already having used `get_viewport()` or something else that depends on it somewhere else in the input method by this point is very likely non-zero.
I see it as rather useless.
If the problem is that `accept_event()` will fail silently, maybe it just needs an error print added? This way you will get an error on wrong usage, and not crash.

I do not see the point in that. It is very clear how `get_viewport` and `set_input_as_handled` operates from the documentation. There should be no confusion as to what the correct usage of it would be. I see no reason as to why the programmer should be exempt from understanding what it is they are actually doing just because they are using a control node, nor do I expect them to use `accept_input` without actually having a reason to do so.

My goal with this pull request is not to protect Godot users from learning Godot by actually reading the documentation and learning what a function does before they use it. It is what should be expected of those getting into game development or a new engine.
The goal is to remove a useless function for those that are capable of gaining the bare minimum level of understanding to use either method in the first place, instead of having the insulting expectation that somewhere, there exists a group of users that place functions they don't know about for reasons they don't know about in places they don't understand. If such a user exists, in my mind they are a fool who would be better off going back and learn what exactly it is they are doing rather than attempt to make everything fool-proof, because their problems won't end with `accept_event` and I certainly don't recommend fool-proofing every possible incorrect usage of every engine construct, because it just isn't possible and will only create better fools. 

I am not trying to cater to the accessibility of a fictitious worst-case user. I believe real solutions should be about solving real problems by real users. I believe `accept_event` fails at this, and would continue to fail even with an error on wrong usage, because real users would not use it like that. In the event they did, I believe they would eventually have the problem-solving skills needed to fix the issue and come out better because of it.

If reading the documentation on what input events are and reading what the functions they use in their code do is too much to ask from someone with the understanding that they would have a lot to learn already in their mind, then this pull request does not apply.

I think that the fact that you have to replace over 300 instances from engine code, this removes a point of configuration from the engine, removing this makes us unable to have `Control::accept_event` be specific, and do special handling that might be distinct from `get_viewport()->set_input_as_handled()`

But I think it's a bit confusing to talk about solving real problems by real users on a PR that deprecates a massively widely used method without a clear need and AFAIK no demand

This isn't about fool-proofing, it's about having clear, concise, and helpful ways for users to perform standard and simple tasks, this method represents a simple, safe, and configurable shorthand for performing this action

I don't believe having these kinds of methods will cause the harms you are arguing it will

But regardless this should be discussed further in a [proposal](https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/) as this is a major change and needs community feedback

Personally I think there's a good point in keeping it separate as a sort of future-proofing/conceptual model type of thing. That one control may accept an event is a neat way of looking at it. 

At the same time, I do think it's stupid to fail silently. Tell the user that they're doing something stupid. Emit a warning into the console or something. Do anything except be silent, because **the user, by writing** `accept_event()`, **intended to do something and is failing to do so**, and they should be informed about that. Failing silently is not helpful to the user, it's letting them down.

What's even more stupid is that this failure in some sense does not need to exist. In practice, this is a method of a Viewport, it needs a Viewport in the tree and it only modifies the state of the Viewport. This Viewport is not an object owned by the Control, publicly or privately, nor is it a method parameter, or linked to the Control in any particularly clear way. When we're calling a method on the Control, we implicitly expect it to be modifying the state of the Control and possibly some explicitly linked state, not that it will bizarrely find and modify some unrelated "3rd party" object somewhere else.

If we were being explicit about the fact that this is an action on the Viewport, not the Control, this same conceptual disconnect would not happen. It wouldn't be possible to call this method without a Viewport, as it is. That doesn't mean you can't still have abstraction or the conceptual idea of a control accepting the message, even if it's useless. Mason's going to hate this suggestion, but something like `Viewport::gui_accept_event(Control acceptor)` is one way of communicating "this node is accepting the event" _and_ being explicit about the fact that this is something done on the Viewport. The interface for a user is still fairly simple, but they need to be certain about the existence of a Viewport, and if you want to do something more complex involving the Viewport and the Control, it's clear to the user that both can very much be modified by the action, and both are explicitly available in the method. 

Another possible solution is of course being explicit about the event, even if there ever exists only one simultaneous input event for one Viewport. Let the event have a reference to the Viewport and call `InputEvent::accept_event()` or `Control::accept_event(InputEvent)` or `Viewport::gui_accept_event(InputEvent, Control)` or something like that. Now it's obvious that what's being modified is the event and linked state to the event, like its issuer. Of course that is a more fundamental architectural change and as such would require far more discussion and yet can rise to inspire no more than a short mention here for that same reason.

Conceptual spaghetti, I think we can agree, is nearly always bad. This is undeniably a case of that, even if it is a convenience method. Whether this is bad enough, or whether any of these alternatives are good enough, to elicit replacing it and replacing a couple lines in a few pages of documentation is another question. It probably could be a proposal with the amount of points I could still discuss yet refrain from doing so here, but it could also be pretty minor. Either way I think it is a good idea to take another look at this ancient solution, the way it is currently is just not very nice.
